headline: Malaysia has been below replacement since 2013; its projection peaks in 2059
context: Malaysia's fertility rate has stayed below the 2.1 replacement level every year since 2013, reaching 1.6 in 2024 with the fewest births in over 40 years. The statistics department's own projection has the population peaking at 42.38 million in 2059, then declining.

cards.big: Malaysia stopped replacing itself in 2013. 2024 brought the fewest babies in over 40 years, and the official projection has the population shrinking from 2059.
cards.sub: The yearly birth drop is reported as a surprise. The decade-long trend, and the peak just ahead, rarely are.

cards.big: The fertility rate was 1.6 in 2024, below the 2.1 needed to hold a population steady, and it has stayed below that line every year since 2013.
cards.sub: About 414,918 babies were born in 2024, the fewest in more than four decades.

cards.big: The statistics department's own projection has the population peaking at 42.38 million in 2059, then declining to 41.43 million by 2070.
cards.sub: Public debate still assumes a forever-growing Malaysia; the official numbers already mark the turn.

cards.big: Fewer births now means fewer workers later. The same trend drives a fast-ageing population: those 65 and older passed 7% in 2021 and head for 14% by about 2048.
cards.sub: A smaller working base must support a larger retired one, the squeeze behind the pension and healthcare bills.

cards.big: Malaysia debates how to raise the birth rate. The fact already set for the next 30 years, the year the population turns down, is the one nobody plans for.
It is like a reservoir whose inflow fell below its outflow years ago. The level still looks high, but the date it starts to drop is already fixed.
A country can plan for a smaller, older population or be surprised by one. Malaysia's own statisticians have named the year; the harder task is saying the forecast out loud.
